name: Paro Tshechu
when: March–April, 11th–15th days of the 2nd Bhutanese month (lunar); 29 Mar–2 Apr 2026, tentatively 18–22 Mar 2027
summary: Paro's five-day spring festival of masked cham dances at Rinpung Dzong, one of the two biggest tshechus in Bhutan. It ends before dawn on the last day with the unrolling of a giant thongdrel of Guru Rinpoche, taken down before sunlight touches it.
body: A tshechu, 'tenth day', is a festival honouring Guru Rinpoche, held in each district on dates set by the lunar calendar. Paro's runs from the 11th to the 15th day of the second Bhutanese month, usually in March or April. It begins with rites inside Rinpung Dzong and moves to the Deyangkha ground beside it, where monks and laymen perform masked dances: the Black Hat dance, the dance of the stags and hounds, the dance of the lords of the cremation grounds and more.

The climax comes before dawn on the last day, when a giant thongdrel, about 20 m wide, showing Guru Rinpoche's eight manifestations is unrolled on the dzong wall. Bhutanese believe that seeing it cleanses sin. It goes up around 3–4 am and comes down early in the morning so that sunlight never falls on it. Families arrive in the dark with flasks of tea.

Between dances, atsaras, masked clowns, joke with the crowd and bless people with wooden phalluses. The festival is a social event as much as a religious one: Bhutanese wear their finest gho and kira, and stalls sell food and toys. Paro's hotels and flights sell out months ahead, so book three to four months in advance. Dates for 2026 were 29 March to 2 April; tentative 2027 dates are 18–22 March. Check current status before you travel.
tips: Reach the ground by 3.30 am on the last day for the thongdrel.
Bring a cushion or mat, a flask and warm layers; mornings are cold in March.
Do not walk across the dance ground or use flash in dancers' faces.

faqs.a: The tentative 2027 dates are 18–22 March, with the thongdrel on the last morning. In 2026 it ran 29 March to 2 April. Dates follow the lunar calendar and are confirmed closer to the time. Check current status before you travel.
Yes. Entry to the festival ground is free, though you must be with your licensed guide and follow dress and photography rules. Hotels in Paro and Thimphu fill early, so book months ahead.

A giant appliqué thangka, here about 20 m wide, showing Guru Rinpoche and his eight manifestations. It is displayed before dawn on the last day and rolled up before sunlight touches it. Seeing it is believed to cleanse sins.

faqs.q: What should I wear to Paro Tshechu?
faqs.a: Smart, modest clothes: long sleeves and long trousers or a long skirt, closed shoes and warm layers for the cold pre-dawn. Some visitors rent a gho or kira in Paro, which locals appreciate.

name: Thimphu Tshechu
when: September–October, 10th–12th days of the 8th Bhutanese month (lunar); 21–23 Sep 2026, tentatively 10–12 Oct 2027
summary: The capital's autumn festival at Tashichho Dzong, three days of masked dances preceded by the Thimphu Drubchen. Among Bhutan's biggest gatherings, it draws families from across western Bhutan in their festival best.
body: The Thimphu Tshechu is held in the grounds of Tashichho Dzong, the seat of Bhutan's government, over three days in the eighth Bhutanese month, usually September or October. It is preceded by days of prayers and by the Thimphu Drubchen, when protective deities are invoked; in 2026 the Drubchen fell on 17 September and the tshechu on 21–23 September.

The dances follow forms said to go back to Guru Rinpoche and to the Zhabdrung and Pema Lingpa traditions. Monks perform the Black Hat dance and other ritual dances in elaborate silk and brocade; laymen perform the more theatrical ones, including the dance of the stags and hounds, based on the story of the saint Milarepa converting a hunter. Atsaras, masked clowns, move through the crowd.

For Bhutanese the festival is also a reunion: families picnic on the slopes, wear new gho and kira and buy from stalls outside. Thimphu's hotels fill quickly and room rates rise. The tentative date for 2027 is 10–12 October. Because the dzong is a working government building, access rules during the festival can change. Check current status before you travel.
tips: Arrive by 8 am for a good place on the stands or slopes.
Pack a hat and sunscreen; autumn sun at 2,300 m is strong by midday.
Book Thimphu rooms three to four months ahead for festival dates.

faqs.a: The tentative 2027 dates are 10–12 October at Tashichho Dzong. In 2026 it ran 21–23 September, with the Thimphu Drubchen on 17 September. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for Thimphu Tshechu?
faqs.a: There is no fee to watch the festival, but you must be with your licensed guide. Your normal SDF and tour costs apply.
Very crowded on the main days, with thousands of Bhutanese and visitors. Arrive early, keep valuables close and agree a meeting point with your guide and group.
Yes, outdoors, without flash and without stepping onto the dance ground. Do not block local spectators with tripods. Photography inside temples remains off limits.

name: Black-necked Crane Festival, Gangtey
when: 11 November each year in recent calendars (2026 and tentatively 2027)
summary: A one-day community festival in the courtyard of Gangtey Goenpa in the Phobjikha valley that welcomes the black-necked cranes back from Tibet, with crane dances by schoolchildren, masked dances, folk songs and conservation messages.
body: The black-necked cranes reach Phobjikha in the last week of October from their breeding grounds on the Tibetan Plateau, and the valley's people treat them as a blessing. Local belief holds that they circle Gangtey Goenpa three times when they arrive. The festival, organised with the Royal Society for Protection of Nature, celebrates their return and raises awareness of conservation.

It is held in the courtyard of Gangtey Goenpa on 11 November in recent calendars, the birthday of the fourth king; some sources give 12 November for earlier years. The highlight is the crane dance, performed by local schoolchildren in black-and-white crane costumes, alongside masked dances, folk songs and plays about protecting the birds. Local stalls sell food and crafts.

Phobjikha has few rooms, so book three to four months ahead. Combine the festival with dawn crane watching at the RSPN viewpoints, keeping well back from the birds. The valley is at about 3,000 m and cold in November, with frosty mornings. Check current status before you travel.
tips: Book Phobjikha rooms by August for 11 November.
Watch cranes at dawn the next morning when the crowds have gone.
Bring binoculars and keep at least 100 m from feeding birds.

faqs.q: When is the Black-necked Crane Festival?
faqs.a: On 11 November in recent years, including the 2026 calendar and the tentative 2027 calendar, at Gangtey Goenpa in Phobjikha. Older sources mention 12 November. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Will I definitely see cranes at the festival?
faqs.a: Very likely. By mid-November most of the season's cranes have arrived in Phobjikha. Viewing is best at dawn and late afternoon from the RSPN viewpoints.
The local community and Gangtey Goenpa, with the Royal Society for Protection of Nature, Bhutan's conservation society that manages the valley's Ramsar wetland.

faqs.q: How cold is Phobjikha in November?
faqs.a: Days are often sunny and 10–14 °C, but mornings and nights drop below freezing. Pack thermals, a down jacket, hat and gloves.
